messages.subject: Optimal Weighing
parts:
Hi Chris, 

I am having a little trouble understanding which option would be appropriate to account for different sampling frequencies. I have attached 2 different cases. 

  • Would it be wise to just use the 'exact' calculation option for cases in general (especially when dataset is not large)? 
                    UD1w <- akde(d20.w1, d20w1.FIT, weights = TRUE, fast = FALSE, PC = "direct")

  • Or specify the 'dt'?  Since the fixes have variability, what would be an optimal dt then (for e.g. in the first dt plot)? 



Thanks in advance!
Soham Mehta

messages.author: 40fd627580dd34f5
messages.subject: Re: Optimal Weighing
parts:
Hi Soham,

The automated choice is pretty good now (in the development branch), and that dt should be reported in a message. It should be the smallest interval adjusted to an integer fraction of the median interval. And if the dataset is small enough, this should automatically switch over to the exact algorithm.

Only in a large dataset with extreme variability in the sampling intervals should the automated choice need to be adjusted.

Best,
Chris

messages.author: 40fd627580dd34f5
messages.subject: Re: Optimal Weighing
parts:
Hi Soham,

The exact algorithm has a computational cost of O(n^3), where n is the number of data points. This is very slow for tens of thousands of location fixes.

The fast algorithm has a computational cost of O(N log(N)), where N is the number of grid points. This is reasonably fast for millions of grid points. However, if you have 1 Hz data and 1 year gaps, then the automated grid intervals will be 1 second and will span the gaps, which can make for an extremely large N. Eventually, you will run out of memory this way.

Best,
Chris

messages.author: 40fd627580dd34f5
messages.subject: Re: Optimal Weighing
parts:
Hi Soham,

With error=FALSE, you should be able to change the pch plot argument to something other than a circle, or the type argument, etc.. Otherwise, this is automated according to the density of points for visibility.

If you run dt.plot() you can see the time intervals in your data, and if some so small that the animal does not move very far in that time span compared to the location error, then you either need a location error model or to thin out the small sampling intervals.

Without HDOP values or calibration data, I would set a prior of around 20-30 meter error for GPS data, as in the vignette example: https://ctmm-initiative.github.io/ctmm/articles/error.html

It is best to setup the error model before outlier detection, otherwise the default error values are being used (e.g., 10 meters), which is likely okay anyhow.

Best,
Chris

messages.author: 40fd627580dd34f5
messages.subject: Re: Optimal Weighing
parts:
Hi Soham,

I don't see any big outliers if those maximum speeds are realistic for your species.

You can/should assign an error model to all the individuals.

When fitting your movement model + location error model, your error estimate increased from the ~20 meter prior to a 40-52 meter posterior estimate. That's taking a couple of hectares from the error-less home-range area estimate (and almost half the diffusion rate estimate) and assigning that to the location error model. Without calibration data and/or more structure in the error model (such as from HDOPs), it's hard to say if this is an appropriate division of the variance. Are there no other columns in the data (DOP, number of satellites, anything)? Are there any data from the same model collar that you can use for calibration (sleeping or dead individuals, testing)? If not, this sounds like the best that you can do.

Best,
Chris

Hi Soham,

You can make the prior more informative by increasing the 'DOF' parameter. For instance:

data(buffalo)
UERE <- uere(buffalo)
UERE$UERE[,'horizontal'] <- 15
UERE$DOF[,'horizontal'] <- 8.5
summary(UERE)
uere(buffalo) <- UERE

This gives you an approximately 10-20 meter 95% credible interval for the prior, though that is not the same thing as a 10-20 meter 95% prediction interval.

Best,
Chris

With error=FALSE, you should be able to change the pch plot argument to something other than a circle, or the type argument, etc.. Otherwise, this is automated according to the density of points for visibility.

If you run dt.plot() you can see the time intervals in your data, and if some so small that the animal does not move very far in that time span compared to the location error, then you either need a location error model or to thin out the small sampling intervals.

Without HDOP values or calibration data, I would set a prior of around 20-30 meter error for GPS data, as in the vignette example: https://ctmm-initiative.github.io/ctmm/articles/error.html

It is best to setup the error model before outlier detection, otherwise the default error values are being used (e.g., 10 meters), which is likely okay anyhow.

Best,
Chris

Hi Soham,

The exact algorithm has a computational cost of O(n^3), where n is the number of data points. This is very slow for tens of thousands of location fixes.

The fast algorithm has a computational cost of O(N log(N)), where N is the number of grid points. This is reasonably fast for millions of grid points. However, if you have 1 Hz data and 1 year gaps, then the automated grid intervals will be 1 second and will span the gaps, which can make for an extremely large N. Eventually, you will run out of memory this way.

Chris

Hi Soham,

The 10-20 credible interval is the uncertainty for the root-mean-square (RMS) location error (a parameter of the error distribution) and not the prediction intervals of the posterior distribution (the range of errors that you tend to see).

If you had to, you could fix the RMS UERE (infinite DOF) and then report the sensitivity, most simply by running at 10 meters and 20 meters.

Best,
Chris

Hi Soham,

You can make the prior more informative by increasing the 'DOF' parameter. For instance:

data(buffalo)
UERE <- uere(buffalo)
UERE$UERE[,'horizontal'] <- 15
UERE$DOF[,'horizontal'] <- 8.5
summary(UERE)
uere(buffalo) <- UERE

This gives you an approximately 10-20 meter 95% credible interval for the prior, though that is not the same thing as a 10-20 meter 95% prediction interval.

Best,
Chris

Hi Soham,

A fixed value is the same as an infinite DOF. The problem that you were running into with small DOFs was that the updated posterior was like something you would only see underneath very dense canopy and brush. The higher the DOF, the less the value will be updated and infinite DOF will not update.

So, in your  case, I would run a plausible range of fixed values and report the sensitivity. One way to do that would be a fixed 15-meter error and then to report how +/-5 meters of error changes your results.

Best,
Chris

The exact algorithm has a computational cost of O(n^3), where n is the number of data points. This is very slow for tens of thousands of location fixes.

The fast algorithm has a computational cost of O(N log(N)), where N is the number of grid points. This is reasonably fast for millions of grid points. A fixed value is the same as an infinite DOF. The problem that you were running into with small DOFs was that the updated posterior was like something you would only see underneath very dense canopy and brush. The higher the DOF, the less the value will be updated and infinite DOF will not update.

Chris

On Saturday, August 5, 2023 at 9:15:32 PM UTC+5:30 chris.h...@gmail.com wrote:
Hi Soham,

The exact algorithm has a computational cost of O(n^3), where n is the number of data points. This is very slow for tens of thousands of location fixes.

The fast algorithm has a computational cost of O(N log(N)), where N is the number of grid points. This is reasonably fast for millions of grid points. However, if you have 1 Hz data and 1 year gaps, then the automated grid intervals will be 1 second and will span the gaps, which can make for an extremely large N. Eventually, you will run out of memory this way.

Best,
Chris

On Saturday, August 5, 2023 at 9:15:32 PM UTC+5:30 chris.h...@gmail.com wrote:
Hi Soham,

The exact algorithm has a computational cost of O(n^3), where n is the number of data points. This is very slow for tens of thousands of location fixes.

The fast algorithm has a computational cost of O(N log(N)), where N is the number of grid points. This is reasonably fast for millions of grid points. However, if you have 1 Hz data and 1 year gaps, then the automated grid intervals will be 1 second and will span the gaps, which can make for an extremely large N. Eventually, you will run out of memory this way.

Best,
Chris

Hi Soham,

The exact algorithm has a computational cost of O(n^3), where n is the number of data points. This is very slow for tens of thousands of location fixes.

The fast algorithm has a computational cost of O(N log(N)), where N is the number of grid points. This is reasonably fast for millions of grid points. However, if you have 1 Hz data and 1 year gaps, then the automated grid intervals will be 1 second and will span the gaps, which can make for an extremely large N. Eventually, you will run out of memory this way.

Best,
Chris

On Saturday, August 5, 2023 at 9:15:32 PM UTC+5:30 chris.h...@gmail.com wrote:
Hi Soham,

The exact algorithm has a computational cost of O(n^3), where n is the number of data points. This is very slow for tens of thousands of location fixes.

The fast algorithm has a computational cost of O(N log(N)), where N is the number of grid points. This is reasonably fast for millions of grid points. However, if you have 1 Hz data and 1 year gaps, then the automated grid intervals will be 1 second and will span the gaps, which can make for an extremely large N. Eventually, you will run out of memory this way.

Best,
Chris

On Saturday, August 5, 2023 at 9:15:32 PM UTC+5:30 chris.h...@gmail.com wrote:
Hi Soham,

The exact algorithm has a computational cost of O(n^3), where n is the number of data points. This is very slow for tens of thousands of location fixes.

The fast algorithm has a computational cost of O(N log(N)), where N is the number of grid points. This is reasonably fast for millions of grid points. However, if you have 1 Hz data and 1 year gaps, then the automated grid intervals will be 1 second and will span the gaps, which can make for an extremely large N. Eventually, you will run out of memory this way.

Best,
Chris

If you had to, you could fix the RMS UERE (infinite DOF) and then report the sensitivity, most simply by running at 10 meters and 20 meters.

You can make the prior more informative by increasing the 'DOF' parameter. For instance:

data(buffalo)
UERE <- uere(buffalo)
UERE$UERE[,'horizontal'] <- 15

summary(UERE)
uere(buffalo) <- UERE

This gives you an approximately 10-20 meter 95% credible interval for the prior, though that is not the same thing as a 10-20 meter 95% prediction interval.

On Saturday, August 5, 2023 at 9:15:32 PM UTC+5:30 chris.h...@gmail.com wrote:
Hi Soham,

The exact algorithm has a computational cost of O(n^3), where n is the number of data points. This is very slow for tens of thousands of location fixes.

The fast algorithm has a computational cost of O(N log(N)), where N is the number of grid points. This is reasonably fast for millions of grid points. However, if you have 1 Hz data and 1 year gaps, then the automated grid intervals will be 1 second and will span the gaps, which can make for an extremely large N. Eventually, you will run out of memory this way.

Best,
Chris
